patient.chief_complaint: 3-week progressive confusion and personality change — HE vs enzalutamide CNS effects vs prostate cancer CNS involvement
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 61-year-old man with NASH cirrhosis and castration-resistant prostate cancer on enzalutamide who presents with 3 weeks of slowly progressive confusion, emotional blunting, and passivity. His wife noticed he was no longer engaged in conversation, was having difficulty following complex discussions, and seemed 'far away.' He had a prior grade 1 HE episode 4 months ago that resolved with rifaximin. His ammonia on admission is 64 µmol/L — only mildly elevated. His EEG shows non-specific slowing. His CT head is negative for metastatic disease. The diagnostic puzzle involves three competing diagnoses for his progressive encephalopathy: (1) HE (mildly elevated ammonia, cirrhosis, prior episode), (2) enzalutamide CNS toxicity (enzalutamide crosses blood-brain barrier; causes fatigue, cognitive decline, and rarely seizures; known adverse effect), and (3) leptomeningeal carcinomatosis from prostate cancer (rare but can present with insidious cognitive decline without obvious focal deficits). The key diagnostic differentiation requires careful attention to the clinical pattern, MRI brain with gadolinium, and therapeutic trial of lactulose.

output.query: Hepatic encephalopathy prognosis in cirrhosis with concurrent advanced cancer

results.title: HE prognosis in patients with concurrent malignancy and cirrhosis
results.summary: Hepatic encephalopathy in patients with concurrent advanced malignancy represents a high-risk group. MELD score and cancer stage are independent predictors. However, HE episodes precipitated by reversible factors (mild hyperammonemia, drug effects) can respond to treatment even in advanced disease. Goals of care discussions should include prognosis from both liver disease and malignancy.

output.summary: Published cohort studies report that HE episodes in patients with concurrent advanced malignancy and cirrhosis can respond to standard ammonia-lowering therapies when precipitated by reversible factors. MELD score and cancer stage are identified as independent prognostic factors in this population in multi-centre registry analyses.

critical_actions: MRI brain with gadolinium is required in cancer patients with progressive cognitive decline — non-contrast CT alone cannot exclude leptomeningeal carcinomatosis
Therapeutic response to lactulose is the definitive diagnostic test when multiple etiologies are possible — leptomeningeal disease and enzalutamide toxicity do not respond to lactulose; HE does
Ammonia 64 µmol/L (mildly elevated) does NOT exclude HE — clinical diagnosis based on symptoms + asterixis + treatment response
Enzalutamide can be continued if HE responds to treatment — HE is the primary diagnosis, not enzalutamide toxicity
contraindicated_actions: Relying on non-contrast CT to exclude leptomeningeal carcinomatosis — MRI with gadolinium required
Stopping enzalutamide without oncology consultation — cancer progression risk
Attributing complete encephalopathy to enzalutamide without ammonia measurement and treatment trial
key_reasoning_points: Three competing diagnoses for cognitive decline in cancer patients on hepatotoxic treatment: HE vs drug CNS toxicity vs CNS metastasis — each requires specific diagnostic approach
MRI brain with gadolinium is the gold standard for leptomeningeal carcinomatosis — non-contrast CT has insufficient sensitivity
Therapeutic lactulose response is diagnostically decisive when multiple etiologies are possible — a test of treatment
Enzalutamide cognitive effects are real but do not cause asterixis or respond to lactulose — the presence of asterixis shifts probability toward metabolic/HE etiology

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rising PSA requires staging workup (which includes MRI brain) — but MRI brain negative for CNS disease; HE is the primary diagnosis confirmed by treatment response; cancer workup should be concurrent, not exclusive

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Enzalutamide cognitive effects do not respond to lactulose; complete recovery with lactulose + rifaximin excludes enzalutamide as primary cause; continue enzalutamide for cancer control
